First, let's find the image of ${b}_{1}$ and ${b}_{2}$ under $T,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}T({b}_{1}) & =T([\begin{aligned}6 \\ -2\end{aligned}])=[\begin{aligned}50 \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\ T({b}_{2}) & =T([\begin{aligned}4 \\ 2\end{aligned}])=[\begin{aligned}10 \\ -20\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

To find the coordinates of $T({b}_{1})$ and $T({b}_{2})$ relative to the basis $B$, we consider the matrix

$$
M=[\begin{aligned}| & | & | & | \\ {b}_{1} & {b}_{2} & T({b}_{1}) & T({b}_{2}) \\ | & | & | & |\end{aligned}].
$$

Now, we reduce the left-hand side to reduced row echelon form using Gaussian elimination. Then, on the right-hand side, we will obtain the $B$-matrix for $T:$

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}6 & 4 & 50 & 10 \\ -2 & 2 & 0 & -20\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{1}:=\frac{1}{6}{R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & \frac{2}{3} & \frac{25}{3} & \frac{5}{3} \\ -2 & 2 & 0 & -20\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+2{R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & \frac{2}{3} & \frac{25}{3} & \frac{5}{3} \\ 0 & \frac{10}{3} & \frac{50}{3} & -\frac{50}{3}\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}:=\frac{3}{10}{R}_{2}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & \frac{2}{3} & \frac{25}{3} & \frac{5}{3} \\ 0 & 1 & 5 & -5\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{1}:={R}_{1}-\frac{2}{3}{R}_{2}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 5 & 5 \\ 0 & 1 & 5 & -5\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we obtain

$$
[\,T\,]_{B}=[\begin{aligned}5 & 5 \\ 5 & -5\end{aligned}].
$$"} {:db/id 17592186124540 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186124349 :question/id #uuid "a2b2d84f-cf3b-52a7-98e0-e659d04697f2" :question/math-academy-id "e-5514"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "823a7d28-5a92-5901-8ee0-e5116df6766b" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186050825}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186125119 :question/id #uuid "41e58550-d329-5f5e-b63a-6c321a9666b5" :question/math-academy-id "q-38087"} {:db/id 17592186125230 :question/id #uuid "c24f4b32-c910-5f42-ae2a-40df84514dc2" :question/math-academy-id "q-82162"} {:db/id 17592186272035 :question/id #uuid "5f968c5f-4250-5488-a34a-4146cd513405" :question/math-academy-id "q-140189"} {:db/id 17592186326725 :question/id #uuid "ade064ac-fc93-5e6f-a92b-aac7997b4ec9" :question/math-academy-id "q-38881"} {:db/id 17592186388660 :question/id #uuid "a09a0529-4a70-5078-acf5-0fcce4d8faaa" :question/math-academy-id "q-140192"} {:db/id 17592186394380 :question/id #uuid "937e6ebd-549c-55e5-b730-8f88d5528f46" :question/math-academy-id "q-82454"}] :knowledge-point/title "Calculating the Image of a Vector Given the Matrix of a Linear Transformation Relative to a Basis"} {:db/id 17592186124349 :question/id #uuid "a2b2d84f-cf3b-52a7-98e0-e659d04697f2" :question/math-academy-id "e-5514" :knowledge-point/_canonical-example [{:db/id 17592186124540 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "823a7d28-5a92-5901-8ee0-e5116df6766b" :knowledge-point/title "Calculating the Image of a Vector Given the Matrix of a Linear Transformation Relative to a Basis"}] :question/problem "Let $\mathcal{B}=\{ \mathbf{b}_1,\mathbf{b}_2 \}$ be a basis of $\mathbb{R}^2$ and let $\mathbf{T}:\mathbb{R}^2 \rightarrow \mathbb{R}^2$ be a linear transformation. To find the coordinates of $T({b}_{1}),$ $T({b}_{2}),$ and $T({b}_{3})$ relative to the basis $B$, we consider the matrix

$$

$$
B={[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1 \\ 1\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -1 \\ 0\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0 \\ 3\end{aligned}]},\,[\,T\,]_{B}=[\begin{aligned}a & -5 & -9 \\ 3 & b & 6 \\ 1 & \frac{4}{3} & c\end{aligned}].
$$

What is the value of $\,a+b+c,\,$ given that  

$$
T([\begin{aligned}x \\ y \\ z\end{aligned}])=[\begin{aligned}x+y+z \\ x+z \\ y-z\end{aligned}]
$$" :question/worked-solution "Let's denote the vectors of $B$ as ${{b}_{1},{b}_{2},{b}_{3}}.$ The $B$-matrix for $T$ is a matrix whose columns are the coordinates of the vectors $T({b}_{1}),$ $T({b}_{2}),$ and $T({b}_{3})$ relative to the basis $B.$

First, let's find the image of ${b}_{1},$ ${b}_{2},$ and ${b}_{3}$ under $T,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}T({b}_{1}) & =T([\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1 \\ 1\end{aligned}])=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2 \\ -2\end{aligned}] \\ T({b}_{2}) & =T([\begin{aligned}2 \\ -1 \\ 0\end{aligned}])=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2 \\ -1\end{aligned}] \\ T({b}_{3}) & =T([\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0 \\ 3\end{aligned}])=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 3 \\ -3\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

To find the coordinates of $T({b}_{1}),$ $T({b}_{2}),$ and $T({b}_{3})$ relative to the basis $B$, we consider the matrix

$$
M=[\begin{aligned}| & | & | & | & | & | \\ {b}_{1} & {b}_{2} & {b}_{3} & T({b}_{1}) & T({b}_{2}) & T({b}_{3}) \\ | & | & | & | & | & |\end{aligned}].
$$

Now, we reduce the left-hand side to reduced row echelon form using Gaussian elimination. Then, on the right-hand side, we will obtain the $B$-matrix for $T:$

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 0 & 1 & 1 & 3 \\ -1 & -1 & 0 & 2 & 2 & 3 \\ 1 & 0 & 3 & -2 & -1 & -3\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}:={R}_{1}+{R}_{2} \\ {R}_{3}:={R}_{3}-{R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 0 & 1 & 1 & 3 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 & 3 & 3 & 6 \\ 0 & -2 & 3 & -3 & -2 & -6\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{1}:={R}_{1}-2{R}_{2} \\ {R}_{3}:=2{R}_{2}+{R}_{3}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 & -5 & -5 & -9 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 & 3 & 3 & 6 \\ 0 & 0 & 3 & 3 & 4 & 6\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{3}:=\frac{1}{3}{R}_{3}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 & -5 & -5 & -9 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 & 3 & 3 & 6 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 1 & \frac{4}{3} & 2\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we obtain

$$
[\,T\,]_{B}=[\begin{aligned}-5 & -5 & -9 \\ 3 & 3 & 6 \\ 1 & \frac{4}{3} & 2\end{aligned}].
$$

Finally, $a=-5,$ $b=3,$ $c=2$ and 

$$
a+b+c=-5+3+2=0.
$$"} {:db/id 17592186124576 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186124383 :question/id #uuid "71ac5a84-d8e8-5de6-8adc-e0172457a772" :question/math-academy-id "e-7249"} :knowledge-point/id transformation. Find $[\,T\,]_{B}\,$ if $\,T({b}_{1})={b}_{2}\,$ and $\,T({b}_{2})=2{b}_{1}.$" :question/worked-solution "Since we have $\,T({b}_{1})={b}_{2}\,$ and $\,T({b}_{2})=2{b}_{1}\,$, we have

$$
[T({b}_{1})]_{B}=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}],\,[T({b}_{2})]_{B}=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 0\end{aligned}].
$$

Now, the $B$-matrix for $T$ is a matrix  whose columns are the coordinates of the vectors $T({b}_{1})$ and $T({b}_{2})$ relative to the basis $B.$ Therefore, we obtain

$$
[\,T\,]_{B}=[\begin{aligned}0 & 2 \\ 1 & 0\end{aligned}].
$$"} {:db/id 17592186392252 :question/id #uuid "a4116c45-97e6-56c3-98ac-05554e466b38" :question/math-academy-id "q-38913"} {:db/id 17592186416398 :question/id #uuid "abf9f8e2-5bef-5f02-8f73-975c228317db" :question/math-academy-id "q-82461" :knowledge-point/_questions [{:db/id 17592186124576 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "6641b2cf-00bc-5542-a566-5b8689f2f2a4" :knowledge-point/title "Finding the Matrix of a Linear Transformation Given the Images of the Basis Vectors"}] :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "2fb9e7d4-7d49-5611-aa8c-f624e6e0dc8d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "7" :db/id 17592186416371} {:answer/id #uuid "6e0f4265-777b-5a68-a83b-4d5ec07516f7" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "5" :db/id 17592186416375} {:answer/id #uuid "9051dc30-494b-5b2b-98d2-22f5ecef3027" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "6" :db/id 17592186416379} {:answer/id #uuid "ab6e7a2c-0fcc-54a7-8cfc-46063d0feef7" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "4" :db/id 17592186416380} {:answer/id #uuid "d806f1c8-7b38-5943-8f66-4ce22d0914ac" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "8" :db/id 17592186416383}] :answer-field/correct {:answer/id #uuid "d806f1c8-7b38-5943-8f66-4ce22d0914ac" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "8" :db/id 17592186416383} :answer-field/id #uuid "cb7d556e-1c97-50dc-be6c-38b9a13c9e90" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493 :db/ident :answer-field.type/radio} :db/id 17592186416394}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487 :db/ident :question.difficulty/moderate} :question/problem "Let $B={{b}_{1},{b}_{2},{b}_{3}}$ be a basis of ${R}^{3}.$ The matrix $[\,T\,]_{B}$ of the linear transformation $T:{R}^{3}\to {R}^{3}$ is given by

$$
[\,T\,]_{B}=[\begin{aligned}a & 1 & 2 \\ -1 & b & -2 \\ 3 & 0 & c\end{aligned}].
$$

Find the value of $\,a+b+c,\,$ given that 

$$
\begin{aligned}T({b}_{1}) & =2{b}_{1}-{b}_{2}+3{b}_{3}, \\ T({b}_{2}) & ={b}_{1}+3{b}_{2}, \\ T({b}_{3}) & =2{b}_{1}-2{b}_{2}+3{b}_{3}.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/worked-solution "First, we write down the coordinates of the images relative to the basis $B:$

$$
[T({b}_{1})]_{B}=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -1 \\ 3\end{aligned}],\,[T({b}_{2})]_{B}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 3 \\ 0\end{aligned}],\,[T({b}_{3})]_{B}=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -2 \\ 3\end{aligned}]
$$

Now, the $B$-matrix for $T$ is a matrix  whose columns are the coordinates of the vectors $T({b}_{1}),$ $T({b}_{2}),$ and $T({b}_{3})$ relative to the basis $B.$ Therefore, we obtain

$$
[\,T\,]_{B}=[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 & 2 \\ -1 & 3 & -2 \\ 3 & 0 & 3\end{aligned}].
$$

Finally, $a=2,$ $b=3,$ $c=3$ and 

$$
a+b+c=2+3+3=8.
$$"} {:db/id 17592186048582} {:db/id 17592186050324} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "1ce3ee34-0bbc-5bf1-8519-a5c6f5ca4be2" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} [{:db/id 17592186125435 :step/content {:db/id 17592186125797 :tutorial/content "What is the matrix of the linear transformation 

$$
[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}]
$$

relative to the basis

$$
[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]
$$

In other words, what is the matrix $[T]_{\mathcal{B}}$ such that 

$$
[\mathbf{T}(\mathbf{x})]_{\mathcal{B}} = [T]_{\mathcal{B}} \cdot[\mathbf{x}]_{\mathcal{B}}?
$$

If you're thinking that the standard matrix 

\[
T=\begin{bmatrix} 3 & 4 \\ -1 & -1 \end{bmatrix}
\]

will work, unfortunately, it does not. For instance, consider the vector [math]\mathbf{x} = \begin{bmatrix} 0 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}[/math], where we have [math][\mathbf{x}]_{\mathcal{B}} = \begin{bmatrix} -1 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}[/math] and [math]\mathbf{T}(\mathbf{x}) = \begin{bmatrix} 4 \\ -1 \end{bmatrix}[/math]. Then:
\begin{align*}
	[\mathbf{T}(\mathbf{x})]_{\mathcal{B}} &= \begin{bmatrix} 9 \\ -5 \end{bmatrix} \\
	T\cdot [\mathbf{x}]_{\mathcal{B}}	&= \begin{bmatrix} 3 & 4 \\ -1 & -1 \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} -1 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} \\
								&= \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 0 \end{bmatrix}.
\end{align*}
Therefore, we have that [math][\mathbf{T}(\mathbf{x})]_{\mathcal{B}} \neq T \cdot[\mathbf{x}]_{\mathcal{B}}[/math].

In fact, the answer is the matrix whose columns are the coordinates of the images of the basis vectors $\mathbf{b}_1, \mathbf{b}_2$ under the transformation relative to the basis:

$$
[\begin{aligned}| & | \\ {[T({b}_{1})]}_{B} & {[T({b}_{2})]}_{B} \\ | & |\end{aligned}]
$$

This matrix is called the **matrix for $\mathbf{T}$ relative to $\mathcal{B}$** or the **$\mathcal{B}$-matrix for $\mathbf{T}.$**

As a result, for the transformation $[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}]$, with respect to the basis 

$$
[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]
$$

we have 

$$
[\begin{aligned}7 \\ -2\end{aligned}]
$$

Now, to write ${\color{red} \mathbf{T} \left( \mathbf{b}_1 \right)}$ and ${\color{blue} \mathbf{T} \left( \mathbf{b}_2 \right) }$ with respect to our basis $\mathcal{B},$ we assume that 

$$
[\begin{aligned}{\alpha }_{1} \\ {\alpha }_{2}\end{aligned}]
$$

where the components $\alpha_1,$ $\alpha_2,$ $\beta_1,$ and $\beta_2$ satisfy

$$
{\color{red}\alpha_1} \mathbf{b}_1+{\color{red}\alpha_2}\mathbf{b}_2 = {\color{red} \mathbf{T} \left( \mathbf{b}_1 \right)}\quad \text{and}\quad {\color{blue}\beta_1}\mathbf{b}_1+{\color{blue}\beta_2} \mathbf{b}_2 = {\color{blue} \mathbf{T} \left( \mathbf{b}_2 \right)}.
$$

Solving these two systems gives

$$
[\begin{aligned}{\alpha }_{1} \\ {\alpha }_{2}\end{aligned}]
$$

Therefore, 

$$
[\begin{aligned}16 & 25 \\ -9 & -14\end{aligned}]
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "065ca75d-4b23-587e-9942-33e8dce0545f" :tutorial/math-academy-id 3583 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "a3b5f073-2339-52af-9f1e-fd0da19753c1" :step/math-academy-id general, consider a basis $\mathcal{B}=\{ \mathbf{b}_1,\mathbf{b}_2,\dots, \mathbf{b}_n \}$ of a vector space $V$ and a linear transformation $\mathbf{T}:V \rightarrow V$. For any $\mathbf{x}\in V$ we have that

$$
\mathbf{x} = x_1\mathbf{b}_1+x_2\mathbf{b}_2+\cdots + x_n\mathbf{b}_n
$$

or, equivalently $[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ ⋮ \\ {x}_{n}\end{aligned}]$.
Then the matrix for $\mathbf{T}$ relative to $\mathcal{B}$ is given by

$$
[\begin{aligned}| & | &  & | \\ [T({b}_{1})]_{B} & [T({b}_{2})]_{B} & ⋯ & [T({b}_{n})]_{B} \\ | & | &  & |\end{aligned}]
$$

Therefore

$$
[\begin{aligned}| & | &  & | \\ [T({b}_{1})]_{B} & [T({b}_{2})]_{B} & ⋯ & [T({b}_{n})]_{B} \\ | & | &  & |\end{aligned}]
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "c40a1e69-05eb-58c1-81f9-0a459daca5ff" :tutorial/math-academy-id 3584 :tutorial/title "The General Case"} :step/id #uuid "c5270756-13af-5caa-bba0-3b34772bfcb9" 	[\mathbf{T}(\mathbf{x})]_{\mathcal{B}} &= \begin{bmatrix} 9 \\ -5 \end{bmatrix} \\

\end{align*}
Therefore, we have that [math][\mathbf{T}(\mathbf{x})]_{\mathcal{B}} \neq T \cdot[\mathbf{x}]_{\mathcal{B}}[/math].

In fact, the answer is the matrix whose columns are the coordinates of the images of the basis vectors $\mathbf{b}_1, \mathbf{b}_2$ under the transformation relative to the basis:

$$
[\begin{aligned}| & | \\ {[T({b}_{1})]}_{B} & {[T({b}_{2})]}_{B} \\ | & |\end{aligned}]

As a result, for the transformation $[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}]$, with respect to the basis 

$$
[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]
$$

we have 

$$
[\begin{aligned}7 \\ -2\end{aligned}]
$$

$$
[\begin{aligned}{\alpha }_{1} \\ {\alpha }_{2}\end{aligned}]
$$

where the components $\alpha_1,$ $\alpha_2,$ $\beta_1,$ and $\beta_2$ satisfy

$$
{\color{red}\alpha_1} \mathbf{b}_1+{\color{red}\alpha_2}\mathbf{b}_2 = {\color{red} \mathbf{T} \left( \mathbf{b}_1 \right)}\quad \text{and}\quad {\color{blue}\beta_1}\mathbf{b}_1+{\color{blue}\beta_2} \mathbf{b}_2 = {\color{blue} \mathbf{T} \left( \mathbf{b}_2 \right)}.
$$

Solving these two systems gives

$$
[\begin{aligned}{\alpha }_{1} \\ {\alpha }_{2}\end{aligned}]
$$

Therefore, 

$$
[\begin{aligned}16 & 25 \\ -9 & -14\end{aligned}]
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "065ca75d-4b23-587e-9942-33e8dce0545f" :tutorial/math-academy-id 3583 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "a3b5f073-2339-52af-9f1e-fd0da19753c1" :step/math-academy-id 20139 :step/next {:db/id 17592186125437}} {:db/id 17592186125797 :tutorial/content "What is the matrix of the linear transformation

"520c428b-7a04-5d55-84b6-a53202f37188" :step/math-academy-id 20143} {:db/id 17592186125438 :step/content {:db/id 17592186125798 :tutorial/content "In general, consider a basis $\mathcal{B}=\{ \mathbf{b}_1,\mathbf{b}_2,\dots, \mathbf{b}_n \}$ of a vector space $V$ and a linear transformation $\mathbf{T}:V \rightarrow V$. For any $\mathbf{x}\in V$ we have that

$$
\mathbf{x} = x_1\mathbf{b}_1+x_2\mathbf{b}_2+\cdots + x_n\mathbf{b}_n
$$

or, equivalently $[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ ⋮ \\ {x}_{n}\end{aligned}]$.
Then the matrix for $\mathbf{T}$ relative to $\mathcal{B}$ is given by

$$
[\begin{aligned}| & | &  & | \\ [T({b}_{1})]_{B} & [T({b}_{2})]_{B} & ⋯ & [T({b}_{n})]_{B} \\ | & | &  & |\end{aligned}]
$$

Therefore

$$
[\begin{aligned}| & | &  & | \\ [T({b}_{1})]_{B} & [T({b}_{2})]_{B} & ⋯ & [T({b}_{n})]_{B} \\ | & | &  & |\end{aligned}]
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "c40a1e69-05eb-58c1-81f9-0a459daca5ff" :tutorial/math-academy-id 3584 :tutorial/title "The General Case"} :step/id #uuid "c5270756-13af-5caa-bba0-3b34772bfcb9" :step/math-academy-id 20142 :step/next {:db/id 17592186125496}} {:db/id 17592186125798 :tutorial/content "In general, consider a basis $\mathcal{B}=\{ \mathbf{b}_1,\mathbf{b}_2,\dots, \mathbf{b}_n \}$ of a vector space $V$ and a linear transformation $\mathbf{T}:V \rightarrow V$. or, equivalently $[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ ⋮ \\ {x}_{n}\end{aligned}]$.
Then the matrix for $\mathbf{T}$ relative to $\mathcal{B}$ is given by

$$
[\begin{aligned}| & | &  & | \\ [T({b}_{1})]_{B} & [T({b}_{2})]_{B} & ⋯ & [T({b}_{n})]_{B} \\ | & | &  & |\end{aligned}]
$$

Therefore

[\begin{aligned}| & | &  & | \\ [T({b}_{1})]_{B} & [T({b}_{2})]_{B} & ⋯ & [T({b}_{n})]_{B} \\ | & | &  & |\end{aligned}]

#uuid "5979cff9-340a-5b78-84fd-5ca3a8c1f370" :question/math-academy-id "q-140374" :question/problem "The basis $B$ of ${R}^{3}$ and the matrix $[\,T\,]_{B}$ of the linear transformation $T:{R}^{3}\to {R}^{3}$ relative to $B$ are given by

$$
B={[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1 \\ 1\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -1 \\ 0\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0 \\ 3\end{aligned}]},\,[\,T\,]_{B}=[\begin{aligned}a & -5 & -9 \\ 3 & b & 6 \\ 1 & \frac{4}{3} & c\end{aligned}].
$$

What is the value of $\,a+b+c,\,$ given that  

$$
T([\begin{aligned}x \\ y \\ z\end{aligned}])=[\begin{aligned}x+y+z \\ x+z \\ y-z\end{aligned}]
$$" :question/worked-solution "Let's denote the vectors of $B$ as ${{b}_{1},{b}_{2},{b}_{3}}.$ The $B$-matrix for $T$ is a matrix whose columns are the coordinates of the vectors $T({b}_{1}),$ $T({b}_{2}),$ and $T({b}_{3})$ relative to the basis $B.$

First, let's find the image of ${b}_{1},$ ${b}_{2},$ and ${b}_{3}$ under $T,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}T({b}_{1}) & =T([\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1 \\ 1\end{aligned}])=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2 \\ -2\end{aligned}] \\ T({b}_{2}) & =T([\begin{aligned}2 \\ -1 \\ 0\end{aligned}])=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2 \\ -1\end{aligned}] \\ T({b}_{3}) & =T([\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0 \\ 3\end{aligned}])=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 3 \\ -3\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

To find the coordinates of $T({b}_{1}),$ $T({b}_{2}),$ and $T({b}_{3})$ relative to the basis $B$, we consider the matrix

$$
M=[\begin{aligned}| & | & | & | & | & | \\ {b}_{1} & {b}_{2} & {b}_{3} & T({b}_{1}) & T({b}_{2}) & T({b}_{3}) \\ | & | & | & | & | & |\end{aligned}].
$$

Now, we reduce the left-hand side to reduced row echelon form using Gaussian elimination. Then, on the right-hand side, we will obtain the $B$-matrix for $T:$

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 0 & 1 & 1 & 3 \\ -1 & -1 & 0 & 2 & 2 & 3 \\ 1 & 0 & 3 & -2 & -1 & -3\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}:={R}_{1}+{R}_{2} \\ {R}_{3}:={R}_{3}-{R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 0 & 1 & 1 & 3 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 & 3 & 3 & 6 \\ 0 & -2 & 3 & -3 & -2 & -6\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{1}:={R}_{1}-2{R}_{2} \\ {R}_{3}:=2{R}_{2}+{R}_{3}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 & -5 & -5 & -9 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 & 3 & 3 & 6 \\ 0 & 0 & 3 & 3 & 4 & 6\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{3}:=\frac{1}{3}{R}_{3}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 & -5 & -5 & -9 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 & 3 & 3 & 6 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 1 & \frac{4}{3} & 2\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we obtain

$$
[\,T\,]_{B}=[\begin{aligned}-5 & -5 & -9 \\ 3 & 3 & 6 \\ 1 & \frac{4}{3} & 2\end{aligned}].
$$

Finally, $a=-5,$ $b=3,$ $c=2$ and 

$$
a+b+c=-5+3+2=0.
$$"} :step/id #uuid "221c00bb-a31d-5347-8911-eac2ff00072c"} {:db/id 17592186416401 :step/content {:db/id 17592186416399 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "0c6e04b1-baff-5b92-8e15-ea0dfbc34cf6" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "[\begin{aligned}5 & 2 \\ -5 & -6\end{aligned}]" :db/id 17592186416366} {:answer/id #uuid "6f10e2cb-3c02-510f-8245-4c4fef2fb57e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "[\begin{aligned}3 & 5 \\ 5 & -5\end{aligned}]" :db/id 17592186416376} {:answer/id #uuid "d919b397-4a17-5c1a-b41c-a4d8613b1b00" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "[\begin{aligned}1 & 5 \\ -4 & -5\end{aligned}]" :db/id 17592186416384} {:answer/id #uuid "e2593c00-382d-5cff-bc6a-79ef94821d99" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "[\begin{aligned}5 & 1 \\ 5 & 0\end{aligned}]" :db/id 17592186416386} {:answer/id #uuid "f8dab090-6ca4-5789-8aba-16cd40d5c9b1" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "[\begin{aligned}5 & 5 \\ 5 & -5\end{aligned}]" :db/id 17592186416390}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186416390} :answer-field/id #uuid "d40ebe53-c259-5fc7-9393-ddb15fac1751" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186416395}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "e8f9b1b9-d1e3-5a9e-a4fd-34ae92b559e5" :question/math-academy-id "q-140360" :question/problem "Let $B$ be a basis of ${R}^{2}$ and let $T:{R}^{2}\to {R}^{2}$ be a linear transformation. Find $[\,T\,]_{B}$, given that

$\,$ $T([\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}])=[\begin{aligned}6x-7y \\ -2x-6y\end{aligned}]\,$ and $\,B={[\begin{aligned}6 \\ -2\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 2\end{aligned}]}.$" :question/worked-solution "Let's denote the vectors of $B$ as ${{b}_{1},{b}_{2}}.$ The $B$-matrix for $T$ is a matrix whose columns are the coordinates of the vectors $T({b}_{1})$ and $T({b}_{2})$ relative to the basis $B.$

First, let's find the image of ${b}_{1}$ and ${b}_{2}$ under $T,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}T({b}_{1}) & =T([\begin{aligned}6 \\ -2\end{aligned}])=[\begin{aligned}50 \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\ T({b}_{2}) & =T([\begin{aligned}4 \\ 2\end{aligned}])=[\begin{aligned}10 \\ -20\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

To find the coordinates of $T({b}_{1})$ and $T({b}_{2})$ relative to the basis $B$, we consider the matrix

$$
M=[\begin{aligned}| & | & | & | \\ {b}_{1} & {b}_{2} & T({b}_{1}) & T({b}_{2}) \\ | & | & | & |\end{aligned}].
$$

Now, we reduce the left-hand side to reduced row echelon form using Gaussian elimination. Then, on the right-hand side, we will obtain the $B$-matrix for $T:$

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}6 & 4 & 50 & 10 \\ -2 & 2 & 0 & -20\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{1}:=\frac{1}{6}{R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & \frac{2}{3} & \frac{25}{3} & \frac{5}{3} \\ -2 & 2 & 0 & -20\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+2{R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & \frac{2}{3} & \frac{25}{3} & \frac{5}{3} \\ 0 & \frac{10}{3} & \frac{50}{3} & -\frac{50}{3}\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}:=\frac{3}{10}{R}_{2}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & \frac{2}{3} & \frac{25}{3} & \frac{5}{3} \\ 0 & 1 & 5 & -5\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{1}:={R}_{1}-\frac{2}{3}{R}_{2}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 5 & 5 \\ 0 & 1 & 5 & -5\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we obtain

$$
[\,T\,]_{B}=[\begin{aligned}5 & 5 \\ 5 & -5\end{aligned}].

$$
\begin{aligned}T({b}_{1}) & =T([\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2\end{aligned}])=[\begin{aligned}7 \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\ T({b}_{2}) & =T([\begin{aligned}-3 \\ 2\end{aligned}])=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ -8\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}

To find the coordinates of $T({b}_{1})$ and $T({b}_{2})$ relative to the basis $B$, we consider the matrix

$$
M=[\begin{aligned}| & | & | & | \\ {b}_{1} & {b}_{2} & T({b}_{1}) & T({b}_{2}) \\ | & | & | & |\end{aligned}].
$$

Now, we reduce the left-hand side to reduced row echelon form using Gaussian elimination. Then, on the right-hand side, we will obtain the $B$-matrix for $T:$

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -3 & 7 & 3 \\ 2 & 2 & 0 & -8\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}:={R}_{2}-2{R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -3 & 7 & 3 \\ 0 & 8 & -14 & -14\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}:=\frac{1}{8}{R}_{2}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -3 & 7 & 3 \\ 0 & 1 & -\frac{7}{4} & -\frac{7}{4}\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{1}:={R}_{1}+3{R}_{2}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & \frac{7}{4} & -\frac{9}{4} \\ 0 & 1 & -\frac{7}{4} & -\frac{7}{4}\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 0 & 2 & -1 & 4 \\ 0 & 3 & 0 & 3 & 9 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 5 & 0 & 0 & 10\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}:=\frac{1}{3}{R}_{2}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 0 & 2 & -1 & 4 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 & 1 & 3 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 5 & 0 & 0 & 10\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{1}:={R}_{1}-2{R}_{2}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 & 0 & -7 & 4 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 & 1 & 3 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 5 & 0 & 0 & 10\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{3}:=\frac{1}{5}{R}_{3}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 & 0 & -7 & 4 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 & 1 & 3 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 0 & 0 & 2\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}

$$

$$" :question/worked-solution "Let's denote the vectors of $B$ as ${{b}_{1},{b}_{2},{b}_{3}}.$ The $B$-matrix for $T$ is a matrix whose columns are the coordinates of the vectors $T({b}_{1}),$ $T({b}_{2}),$ and $T({b}_{3})$ relative to the basis $B.$

$$

$$

$$

$$

:question/math-academy-id "q-82461" :question/problem "Let $B={{b}_{1},{b}_{2},{b}_{3}}$ be a basis of ${R}^{3}.$ The matrix $[\,T\,]_{B}$ of the linear transformation $T:{R}^{3}\to {R}^{3}$ is given by

$$
[\,T\,]_{B}=[\begin{aligned}a & 1 & 2 \\ -1 & b & -2 \\ 3 & 0 & c\end{aligned}].
$$

Find the value of $\,a+b+c,\,$ given that 

$$
\begin{aligned}T({b}_{1}) & =2{b}_{1}-{b}_{2}+3{b}_{3}, \\ T({b}_{2}) & ={b}_{1}+3{b}_{2}, \\ T({b}_{3}) & =2{b}_{1}-2{b}_{2}+3{b}_{3}.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/worked-solution "First, we write down the coordinates of the images relative to the basis $B:$

$$
[T({b}_{1})]_{B}=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -1 \\ 3\end{aligned}],\,[T({b}_{2})]_{B}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 3 \\ 0\end{aligned}],\,[T({b}_{3})]_{B}=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -2 \\ 3\end{aligned}]
$$

Now, the $B$-matrix for $T$ is a matrix  whose columns are the coordinates of the vectors $T({b}_{1}),$ $T({b}_{2}),$ and $T({b}_{3})$ relative to the basis $B.$ Therefore, we obtain

$$
[\,T\,]_{B}=[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 & 2 \\ -1 & 3 & -2 \\ 3 & 0 & 3\end{aligned}].
$$

Finally, $a=2,$ $b=3,$ $c=3$ and 

$$
a+b+c=2+3+3=8.
$$"} :step/id #uuid "fc9d50c6-34cb-59b8-909c-50ceb04dbf99" :step/next {:db/id 17592186416403}} {:db/id 17592186416403 :step/content {:db/id 17592186416396 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "160cf1c3-ac0f-5878-aa13-d5ddd7963cf2" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "3" :db/id 17592186416367} {:answer/id #uuid "1d6e6bfd-9b54-517b-b0e0-a62d79b1f20a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-3" :db/id 17592186416369} {:answer/id #uuid "5711295d-197b-58b6-9e28-191b003214aa" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-10" :db/id 17592186416372} {:answer/id #uuid "582cb2d5-d3fc-5e12-b72f-d8cfda5e904d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "5" :db/id 17592186416373} {:answer/id #uuid "83656066-e5fe-596a-a8ca-783daf5d23d8" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-4" :db/id 17592186416377}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186416377} :answer-field/id #uuid "55345e60-62bc-5001-9ca7-f576705f2f04" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186416392}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "2fc0336a-ad5e-573a-ac70-a523b483c681" :question/math-academy-id "q-82488" :question/problem "The basis $B$ of ${R}^{3}$ and the matrix $[\,T\,]_{B}$ of the linear transformation $T:{R}^{3}\to {R}^{3}$ relative to $B$ are given by

$$

$$" :question/worked-solution "Let's denote the vectors of $B$ as ${{b}_{1},{b}_{2},{b}_{3}}.$ The $B$-matrix for $T$ is a matrix whose columns are the coordinates of the vectors $T({b}_{1}),$ $T({b}_{2}),$ and $T({b}_{3})$ relative to the basis $B.$

To find the coordinates of $T({b}_{1}),$ $T({b}_{2}),$ and $T({b}_{3})$ relative to the basis $B$, we consider the matrix

$$

$$

$$

**not** a solution to this equation?" :question/worked-solution "Assuming $y={e}^{\lambda x}$ and differentiating $y$ with respect to $x$ gives

$$
{y}^{′}=\lambda {e}^{\lambda x},\,{y}^{″}={\lambda }^{2}{e}^{\lambda x}.
$$

Substituting the above into our differential equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{\lambda }^{2}{e}^{\lambda x}+{e}^{\lambda x} & =0 \\ {e}^{\lambda x}({\lambda }^{2}+1) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

The auxiliary equation is therefore

$$
{\lambda }^{2}+1=0.
$$

 

Solving the auxiliary equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\lambda }^{2}+1 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2} & =-1 \\ \lambda  & =\pm \text{i}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, $\lambda =\pm \text{i}$ are the purely imaginary roots of the auxiliary equation. 

Therefore, any linear combination of the functions $\text{Re}({e}^{\text{i}x})=\operatorname{cos}⁡x$ and $\text{Im}({e}^{\text{i}x})=\operatorname{sin}⁡x$ is a solution to the original differential equation. 

Among the given options, only $\operatorname{sin}⁡2x$ is not a solution."} {:db/id 17592186265887 :question/id #uuid "58474b39-7f22-54e5-91df-f41937199af6" :question/math-academy-id "q-130336"} :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485 :db/ident :question.difficulty/easy} :question/problem "Find the general solution to the equation

$$
\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}-6\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+13y=0.
$$" :question/worked-solution "Let $y={e}^{\lambda x}.$ Differentiating $y$ with respect to $x$ gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\lambda {e}^{\lambda x},\,\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}={\lambda }^{2}{e}^{\lambda x}.
$$

Substituting the above into our differential equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{\lambda }^{2}{e}^{\lambda x}-6\lambda {e}^{\lambda x}+13{e}^{\lambda x} & =0 \\ {e}^{\lambda x}({\lambda }^{2}-6\lambda +13) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

The auxiliary equation is therefore

$$
{\lambda }^{2}-6\lambda +13=0.
$$

The auxiliary equation can be solved by completing the square:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\lambda }^{2}-6\lambda +13 & =0 \\ ({\lambda }^{2}-6\lambda +9)-9+13 & =0 \\ (\lambda -3)^{2}+4 & =0 \\ (\lambda -3)^{2} & =-4 \\ \lambda -3 & =\pm 2\text{i} \\ \lambda  & =3\pm 2\text{i}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the general solution to the differential equation is

$$
\begin{aligned}y & ={e}^{3x}(P\operatorname{cos}⁡2x+Q\operatorname{sin}⁡2x).\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186357482 :question/id #uuid "1a885511-1dcf-5606-836f-b33f26907c6e" :question/math-academy-id "q-90802" :knowledge-point/_questions [{:db/id 17592186087778 :knowledge-point/id #uuid :topic/id #uuid "917bf85e-7253-5a9c-8395-ebac6e9e50d7" :topic/math-academy-id 880} :activity/steps [{:db/id 17592186088647 :step/content {:db/id 17592186088942 :tutorial/content "Sometimes, the characteristic equation of a second-order homogeneous ODE has **complex roots**. Let's see how to find the solution in this case.

We will solve the following differential equation:

$$
\frac{\textrm{d}^2 y}{\textrm{d} x^2} + 4y =0.
$$

**Step 1:** Find the characteristic equation.

Assuming a solution of the form $y=e^{\lambda x},$ we find the derivatives:

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}x} = \lambda e^{\lambda x}, \qquad \dfrac{\textrm{d}^2y}{\textrm{d}x^2} = \lambda^2 e^{\lambda x}.
$$

Substituting these into the ODE gives the **characteristic equation**:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\lambda }^{2}{e}^{\lambda x}+4{e}^{\lambda x} & =0 \\ {e}^{\lambda x}({\lambda }^{2}+4) & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}+4 & =0\,(\text{since }{e}^{\lambda x}\ne 0).\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 2:** Solve for the characteristic roots.

$$
\begin{aligned}{\lambda }^{2} & =-4 \\ \lambda  & =\pm \sqrt{-4} \\ \lambda  & =\pm 2\text{i}.\end{aligned}
$$

The roots are a *complex conjugate pair*. Since the roots are distinct, the general solution is a linear combination of the corresponding exponentials:

$$
y = Ae^{2\textrm{i}x} + Be^{-2\textrm{i}x}.
$$

On the next slide, we will use *Euler's formula* to convert this into a more useful real-valued form." :tutorial/id #uuid "18a414e1-5fae-5260-8980-5971fbd844e3" :tutorial/math-academy-id 4052 {:db/id 17592186265886} {:db/id 17592186265887} {:db/id 17592186335736} {:db/id 17592186357483} {:db/id 17592186357484}] :knowledge-point/title "Identifying Non-Solutions of a Second-Order Homogeneous ODEs"} :step/id #uuid "59826183-4e40-52cf-85bf-49e587ced10a" :step/math-academy-id 24235} {:db/id 17592186088650 :step/content {:db/id 17592186088943 :tutorial/content "Sometimes, the characteristic equation of a second-order homogeneous ODE may have complex solutions. In such cases, the general solution will initially involve complex exponentials.

For example, suppose that we want to solve the following differential equation:

$$
\frac{\textrm{d}^2 y}{\textrm{d} x^2} - 6 \frac{\textrm{d} y}{\textrm{d} x} + 18y =0.
$$

Assuming a solution of the form $y=e^{\lambda x}$, we get the **characteristic equation**:

$$
\lambda^2 - 6\lambda + 18 =0.
$$

We can solve this by *completing the square*:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\lambda }^{2}-6\lambda +18 & =0 \\ ({\lambda }^{2}-6\lambda +9)-9+18 & =0 \\ (\lambda -3)^{2}+9 & =0 \\ (\lambda -3)^{2} & =-9 \\ \lambda -3 & =\pm 3\text{i} \\ \lambda  & =3\pm 3\text{i}\end{aligned}
$$

The two complex roots are $\lambda_1 = 3 + 3\textrm{i}$ and $\lambda_2 = 3 - 3\textrm{i}.$

The general solution is therefore

$$
y = Ae^{(3 + 3 \textrm{i})x} + Be^{(3 - 3 \textrm{i})x}.
$$

Next, we will use *Euler's formula* to rewrite this solution in a form that does not involve complex numbers." :tutorial/id #uuid "d2be766f-b054-5431-aaa5-32c2129b9d92" :tutorial/math-academy-id 4053 :tutorial/title "Second-Order Homogeneous ODEs: Characteristic Equation Has Complex Roots"} :step/id #uuid "31b88c4c-e4b0-5b75-8e76-d8013e805d0f" :step/math-academy-id 24236 :step/next {:db/id 17592186088825}} {:db/id 17592186088651 :step/content {:db/id 17592186087777 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186087597 :question/id #uuid "7aa1ff4a-2263-5c99-97dd-d6fcada8bfc0" :question/math-academy-id "e-6597"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "191e98e0-aa31-5dd9-a735-6580d29ad287" :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186088234} {:db/id 17592186088235} {:db/id 17592186265847} {:db/id 17592186357480} {:db/id 17592186357481} {:db/id 17592186424417} {:db/id 17592186424420}] :knowledge-point/title "Finding the Complex Solutions of a Characteristic Equation"} :step/id #uuid "22d3be62-0495-564f-8728-c69a96ff20e8" :step/math-academy-id 24237 :step/next {:db/id 17592186088652}} {:db/id 17592186088652 :step/content {:db/id 17592186087778 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186087598 :question/id #uuid "04253a00-f441-58d8-b97e-f7935ae5c7c6" :question/math-academy-id "e-6598"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "2999a565-bf64-5246-9fee-54cecc9e79ff" :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186088352} {:db/id 17592186088353} {:db/id 17592186265848} {:db/id 17592186265882} {:db/id 17592186348068} {:db/id 17592186357482} {:db/id 17592186424419} {:db/id 17592186424422}] :knowledge-point/title "Finding the General Solution When the Characteristic Equation Has Complex Roots"} :step/id #uuid "87a6e8c8-6061-5698-9cbf-e13d800b6a02" :step/math-academy-id 24238 :step/next {:db/id 17592186088649}} {:db/id 17592186088666 :step/content {:db/id 17592186088957 :tutorial/content "In general, if the characteristic equation of a second-order homogeneous ODE has **imaginary roots** 

$$
\lambda = \pm b\textrm{i},
$$

then the *general solution* is

$$
y(x) = Ae^{\textrm{i} b x} + B e^{-\textrm{i} bx}.
$$

Using *Euler's formula*, the above can be simplified to

$$
y(x) = P \cos bx + Q \sin bx,
$$

where $P = A+B$ and $Q=\textrm{i} (A-B).$

Let's take a look at another example." :tutorial/id #uuid "0cc2f848-e126-5ee8-84ea-809e08a92dff" :tutorial/math-academy-id 4162 :tutorial/title "A Shortcut When the Characteristic Equation Has Imaginary Roots"} :step/id #uuid "e724fe89-8251-5f08-9463-a1bf1a894289" :step/math-academy-id 25327 :step/next {:db/id 17592186088648}} {:db/id 17592186088667 :step/content {:db/id 17592186088958 :tutorial/content "In general, if the characteristic equation of a second-order homogeneous ODE has **complex conjugate roots** 

$$
\lambda = a \pm b\textrm{i},
$$

 then the *general solution* is

$$
y(x) = Ae^{(a+b\textrm{i})x} + B e^{(a-b\textrm{i})x}.
$$

Using *Euler's formula*, we can expand and group the terms:

$$
y(x) = e^{ax} \left[ (A+B)\cos bx + \textrm{i}(A-B)\sin bx \right].
$$

This simplifies to

$$
y(x) = e^{ax} \left( P \cos bx + Q \sin bx \right)
$$

where $P = A+B$ and $Q=\textrm{i} (A-B).$

Let's take a look at another example" :tutorial/id #uuid "922b0814-7e51-5155-9464-ccf52671087e" :tutorial/math-academy-id 4163 :tutorial/title "A Shortcut When the Characteristic Equation Has Complex Roots"} :step/id #uuid "c889c748-9b68-50fe-a9f2-7282493522dd" :step/math-academy-id 25328 :step/next {:db/id 17592186088651}} {:db/id 17592186088825 :step/content {:db/id 17592186088863 :tutorial/content "Recall that our general solution is

$$
y = Ae^{(3 + 3 \textrm{i})x} + Be^{(3 - 3 \textrm{i})x}.
$$

Our goal is to simplify this to find the **real-valued general solution**. We can do this using **Euler's formula**, which states that 

$$
e^{\textrm{i}\theta} = \cos{\theta} + \textrm{i}\sin{\theta}.
$$

First, we use the law of exponents to separate the real and imaginary parts in the exponential:

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =A{e}^{3x}{e}^{3\text{i}x}+B{e}^{3x}{e}^{-3\text{i}x} \\  & ={e}^{3x}(A{e}^{3\text{i}x}+B{e}^{-3\text{i}x}).\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we apply Euler's formula with $\theta = 3x$:

$$
\begin{aligned}y & ={e}^{3x}(A(\operatorname{cos}⁡3x+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡3x)+B(\operatorname{cos}⁡3x-\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡3x)) \\  & ={e}^{3x}((A+B)\operatorname{cos}⁡3x+\text{i}(A-B)\operatorname{sin}⁡3x).\end{aligned}
$$

Since $A$ and $B$ are arbitrary constants, we can define new arbitrary constants $P=A+B$ and $Q=\textrm{i}(A-B).$ The general solution becomes:

$$
\bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{y = e^{3x}(P\cos{3 x} + Q\sin{3 x}).}
$$

This is the final form of the solution, written entirely with real-valued functions.

So, for example,

$$

Let's see how to find the solution in this case.

We will solve the following differential equation:

$$
\frac{\textrm{d}^2 y}{\textrm{d} x^2} + 4y =0.
$$

**Step 1:** Find the characteristic equation.

Assuming a solution of the form $y=e^{\lambda x},$ we find the derivatives:

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}x} = \lambda e^{\lambda x}, \qquad \dfrac{\textrm{d}^2y}{\textrm{d}x^2} = \lambda^2 e^{\lambda x}.
$$

Substituting these into the ODE gives the **characteristic equation**:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\lambda }^{2}{e}^{\lambda x}+4{e}^{\lambda x} & =0 \\ {e}^{\lambda x}({\lambda }^{2}+4) & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}+4 & =0\,(\text{since }{e}^{\lambda x}\ne 0).\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 2:** Solve for the characteristic roots.

$$
\begin{aligned}{\lambda }^{2} & =-4 \\ \lambda  & =\pm \sqrt{-4} \\ \lambda  & =\pm 2\text{i}.\end{aligned}
$$

The roots are a *complex conjugate pair*. Since the roots are distinct, the general solution is a linear combination of the corresponding exponentials:

$$
y = Ae^{2\textrm{i}x} + Be^{-2\textrm{i}x}.
$$

In such cases, the general solution will initially involve complex exponentials.

For example, suppose that we want to solve the following differential equation:

$$
\frac{\textrm{d}^2 y}{\textrm{d} x^2} - 6 \frac{\textrm{d} y}{\textrm{d} x} + 18y =0.
$$

Assuming a solution of the form $y=e^{\lambda x}$, we get the **characteristic equation**:

$$
\lambda^2 - 6\lambda + 18 =0.
$$

We can solve this by *completing the square*:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\lambda }^{2}-6\lambda +18 & =0 \\ ({\lambda }^{2}-6\lambda +9)-9+18 & =0 \\ (\lambda -3)^{2}+9 & =0 \\ (\lambda -3)^{2} & =-9 \\ \lambda -3 & =\pm 3\text{i} \\ \lambda  & =3\pm 3\text{i}\end{aligned}
$$

The two complex roots are $\lambda_1 = 3 + 3\textrm{i}$ and $\lambda_2 = 3 - 3\textrm{i}.$

The general solution is therefore

$$
y = Ae^{(3 + 3 \textrm{i})x} + Be^{(3 - 3 \textrm{i})x}.
$$

Next, we will use *Euler's formula* to rewrite this solution in a form that does not involve complex numbers." :tutorial/id #uuid "d2be766f-b054-5431-aaa5-32c2129b9d92" :tutorial/math-academy-id 4053 :tutorial/title "Second-Order Homogeneous ODEs: Characteristic Equation Has Complex Roots"} :step/id #uuid "31b88c4c-e4b0-5b75-8e76-d8013e805d0f" :step/math-academy-id 24236 :step/next {:db/id 17592186088825}} {:db/id 17592186088649 :step/content {:db/id 17592186087776 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186087596 :question/id #uuid "b22fa1be-4c82-5dbf-b5fe-5cbb42c0c646" :question/math-academy-id "e-6596"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "092a6c8c-7bea-5c53-88ac-f5dc8b16c357" :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186088236} {:db/id 17592186088237} {:db/id 17592186265884} {:db/id 17592186265886} {:db/id 17592186265887} {:db/id 17592186335736} {:db/id 17592186357483} {:db/id 17592186357484}] :knowledge-point/title "Identifying Non-Solutions of a Second-Order Homogeneous ODEs"} :step/id #uuid "59826183-4e40-52cf-85bf-49e587ced10a" :step/math-academy-id 24235} {:db/id 17592186088943 :tutorial/content "Sometimes, the characteristic equation of a second-order homogeneous ODE may have complex solutions. In such cases, the general solution will initially involve complex exponentials.

For example, suppose that we want to solve the following differential equation:

$$
\frac{\textrm{d}^2 y}{\textrm{d} x^2} - 6 \frac{\textrm{d} y}{\textrm{d} x} + 18y =0.
$$

Assuming a solution of the form $y=e^{\lambda x}$, we get the **characteristic equation**:

$$
\lambda^2 - 6\lambda + 18 =0.
$$

We can solve this by *completing the square*:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\lambda }^{2}-6\lambda +18 & =0 \\ ({\lambda }^{2}-6\lambda +9)-9+18 & =0 \\ (\lambda -3)^{2}+9 & =0 \\ (\lambda -3)^{2} & =-9 \\ \lambda -3 & =\pm 3\text{i} \\ \lambda  & =3\pm 3\text{i}\end{aligned}
$$

The two complex roots are $\lambda_1 = 3 + 3\textrm{i}$ and $\lambda_2 = 3 - 3\textrm{i}.$

The general solution is therefore

$$
y = Ae^{(3 + 3 \textrm{i})x} + Be^{(3 - 3 \textrm{i})x}.
$$

Next, we will use *Euler's formula* to rewrite this solution in a form that does not involve complex numbers." :tutorial/id #uuid "d2be766f-b054-5431-aaa5-32c2129b9d92" :tutorial/math-academy-id 4053 :tutorial/title "Second-Order Homogeneous ODEs: Characteristic Equation Has Complex Roots"} {:db/id 17592186088825 :step/content {:db/id 17592186088863 :tutorial/content "Recall that our general solution is

$$
y = Ae^{(3 + 3 \textrm{i})x} + Be^{(3 - 3 \textrm{i})x}.
$$

Our goal is to simplify this to find the **real-valued general solution**. We can do this using **Euler's formula**, which states that 

$$
e^{\textrm{i}\theta} = \cos{\theta} + \textrm{i}\sin{\theta}.
$$

First, we use the law of exponents to separate the real and imaginary parts in the exponential:

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =A{e}^{3x}{e}^{3\text{i}x}+B{e}^{3x}{e}^{-3\text{i}x} \\  & ={e}^{3x}(A{e}^{3\text{i}x}+B{e}^{-3\text{i}x}).\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we apply Euler's formula with $\theta = 3x$:

$$
\begin{aligned}y & ={e}^{3x}(A(\operatorname{cos}⁡3x+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡3x)+B(\operatorname{cos}⁡3x-\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡3x)) \\  & ={e}^{3x}((A+B)\operatorname{cos}⁡3x+\text{i}(A-B)\operatorname{sin}⁡3x).\end{aligned}
$$

Since $A$ and $B$ are arbitrary constants, we can define new arbitrary constants $P=A+B$ and $Q=\textrm{i}(A-B).$ The general solution becomes:

$$
\bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{y = e^{3x}(P\cos{3 x} + Q\sin{3 x}).}
$$

This is the final form of the solution, written entirely with real-valued functions.

So, for example,

$$
y(x) = e^{3x}(5\cos{3 x} - \sin{3 x}),
$$

corresponding to $P=5$ and $Q=-1,$ is a solution of the given differential equation. On the other hand,

$$
y(x) =  e^{3x}(\cos{5 x} - \sin{3 x})
$$

is *not* a solution because it contains a function $e^{3x}\cos{5x},$ which is not included in the above form representing the general solution." :tutorial/id #uuid $$
\begin{aligned}a=\overset{\to }{OA}=[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 4 \\ -2 \\ 2\end{aligned}],\,b=\overset{\to }{OB}=[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 0 \\ -1 \\ -4\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}

$$

:activity/steps [{:db/id 17592186134648 :step/content {:db/id 17592186135038 :tutorial/content "The **Cauchy-Schwarz Inequality** (sometimes called the **Cauchy-Bunyakovsky-Schwarz Inequality**) provides a connection between dot products and norms. It states that for any two vectors $\mathbf{u}$ and $\mathbf{v}$ in $\mathbb{R}^n$, we have the inequality

$$
\vert \mathbf{u} \cdot \mathbf{v} \vert \leq \Vert \mathbf{u} \Vert \Vert \mathbf{v} \Vert.
$$

In other words, the absolute value of the dot product is no more than the product of the norms.

For instance, if $[\begin{aligned}3 \\ -4\end{aligned}]$ and $[\begin{aligned}5 \\ 12\end{aligned}]$ then 

$$
\begin{aligned}|u\cdot v| & \le ‖u‖\cdot ‖v‖ \\ |3\cdot 5+(-4)\cdot 12| & \le \sqrt{{3}^{2}+(-4)^{2}}\sqrt{{5}^{2}+{12}^{2}} \\ |-33| & \le 5\cdot 13 \\ 33 & \le 65.\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

**Note:** An easy trick to remember the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality is to think of the formula for the dot product:

$$
\mathbf u \cdot \mathbf v = \Vert \mathbf u \Vert \Vert \mathbf v \Vert \cos \theta
$$

Because $\vert \cos \theta \vert \leq 1,$ we can see that

$$
\vert \mathbf{u} \cdot \mathbf{v} \vert \leq \Vert \mathbf{u} \Vert \Vert \mathbf{v} \Vert.
$$

**Watch out!** The above trick is only a mnemonic trick, *not* an actual proof of the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality. The formula $\mathbf u \cdot \mathbf v = \Vert \mathbf u \Vert \Vert \mathbf v \Vert \cos \theta$ is actually a *consequence* of the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality, so a proof of the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality cannot use the formula." :tutorial/id #uuid "7dd99f48-bbdd-5c22-b5b5-f540eed16b92" :tutorial/math-academy-id 3609 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "37742cc9-b4c6-528d-a58c-980bbc6f6f0f" :step/math-academy-id 20206 :step/next {:db/id 17592186134649}} {:db/id 17592186134649 :step/content {:db/id 17592186133773 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186133582 :question/id #uuid "77b63ba5-410b-536c-8ed0-92c895097cc9" :question/math-academy-id "e-5554"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "7ec34a19-988a-5421-8c05-6bb4c5a9e366" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186048849}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186134218} {:db/id 17592186134263} {:db/id 17592186272088} {:db/id 17592186272089} {:db/id 17592186326765} {:db/id 17592186326886} {:db/id 17592186342150}] :knowledge-point/title "Determining a Minimum Possible Value Using the Cauchy-Schwarz Inequality"} :step/id #uuid "f5ab144b-fcb0-51fc-bdfa-3c957620d966" :step/math-academy-id 20207 :step/next {:db/id 17592186134650}} {:db/id 17592186134650 :step/content {:db/id 17592186135039 :tutorial/content "Now, using the dot product, we can define the angle $\theta$ between two vectors $\mathbf{u}$ and $\mathbf{v}$ in $\mathbb{R}^n$, where $n \ge 2$.

![](images/82/8244d121c65d655f42378c68e1a197528fb2db60a3890b3842e3c93692d88071.png)

To do that, we say that $\cos\theta$ will be equal to the ratio of the two sides of the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality, as follows:

$$
\cos\theta	=	\dfrac{\mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{v}}{\Vert \mathbf{u} \Vert \cdot \Vert \mathbf{v} \Vert}
$$

Notice that this formula is completely analogous to the formula for the angle between two vectors in two-dimensional or three-dimensional space. It only works for non-zero vectors (otherwise, we will be dividing by zero).

Since the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality guarantees that $|\mathbf{u} \cdot \mathbf{v}| \leq \| \mathbf{u} \| \cdot \| \mathbf{v} \|$, we get

$$
-1 \leq \dfrac{\mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{v}}{\Vert \mathbf{u} \Vert \cdot \Vert \mathbf{v} \Vert} \leq 1,
$$

which means that $\theta$ can be found given any two non-zero $\mathbf{u}$ and $\mathbf{v}$." :tutorial/id #uuid "fb193109-edd9-56c5-a643-2472eb776c80" :tutorial/math-academy-id 3610 :tutorial/title "The Angle Between Two Vectors"} :step/id #uuid "26f7bbc7-420d-5194-a4cc-342313c26a2f" :step/math-academy-id 20208 :step/next {:db/id 17592186134651}} {:db/id 17592186134651 :step/content {:db/id 17592186133774 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186133583 :question/id #uuid "763f7e8e-081a-57ad-825f-601a38fe3984" :question/math-academy-id "e-5555"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "6bde92b0-4e98-5c2e-848e-7a5febc848ae" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186050336}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186134294} {:db/id 17592186134295} {:db/id 17592186272090} {:db/id 17592186326849} {:db/id 17592186326850} {:db/id 17592186326851} {:db/id 17592186326852} {:db/id 17592186326853} {:db/id 17592186326887} {:db/id 17592186414662} {:db/id 17592186414663}] :knowledge-point/title "Finding the Acute Angle Between Two Vectors"} :step/id #uuid "16edcc5a-a81b-54dc-93af-a242d90ab883" :step/math-academy-id 20209 :step/next {:db/id 17592186134720}} {:db/id 17592186134652 :step/content {:db/id 17592186135041 :tutorial/content "Now, let's prove the general statement of the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality for vectors $\mathbf{u}, \mathbf{v} \in \mathbb{R}^n\mathbin{:}$

$$
\vert \mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{v} \vert \leq \Vert \mathbf{u} \Vert \Vert \mathbf{v} \Vert
$$

To start, let $t\in\mathbb{R}$ be any number, and consider the vector $t\mathbf{u}+\mathbf{v}.$ Since $\Vert t\mathbf{u} + \mathbf{v} \Vert \geq 0,$ using the definition and properties of the dot product, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}‖tu+v{‖}^{2} & \ge 0 \\ (tu+v)\cdot (tu+v) & \ge 0 \\ {t}^{2}(u\cdot u)+t(u\cdot v)+t(v\cdot u)+(v\cdot v) & \ge 0 \\ {t}^{2}‖u{‖}^{2}+2t(u\cdot v)+‖v{‖}^{2} & \ge 0.\end{aligned}
$$

In the last line above, we have a quadratic with the coefficients $a=\Vert \mathbf{u} \Vert^2,$ $b=2\left( \mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{v} \right),$ and $c=\Vert \mathbf{v} \Vert^2.$

Since the quadratic is greater than or equal to zero, its discriminant must be less than or equal to zero, $\mathcal{D} \leq 0.$ Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}D & \le 0 \\ {b}^{2}-4ac & \le 0 \\ {(2(u\cdot v))}^{2}-4\cdot ‖u{‖}^{2}\cdot ‖v{‖}^{2} & \le 0 \\ 4{(u\cdot v)}^{2}-4‖u{‖}^{2}‖v{‖}^{2} & \le 0 \\ {(u\cdot v)}^{2} & \le ‖u{‖}^{2}‖v{‖}^{2} \\ \sqrt{{(u\cdot v)}^{2}} & \le \sqrt{‖u{‖}^{2}‖v{‖}^{2}} \\ |u\cdot v| & \le ‖u‖‖v‖.\end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "60d5d1df-43c6-5f0a-9f65-0bf4f078cff0" :tutorial/math-academy-id 3614 :tutorial/title "Algebraic Proof of the Schwarz Inequality"} :step/id #uuid "1fa328eb-e089-5fa4-8c20-b79162bc8781" :step/math-academy-id 20213} {:db/id 17592186134720 :step/content {:db/id 17592186133816 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186133631 :question/id #uuid "0562751a-55be-5fd1-83d2-11795ba7a052" :question/math-academy-id "e-5910"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "7b56b45b-94dd-5ba1-aae6-6b17cffaf532" :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186134328} {:db/id 17592186134331} {:db/id 17592186272094} {:db/id 17592186272095} {:db/id 17592186342151} {:db/id 17592186342154} {:db/id 17592186342157} {:db/id 17592186342163}] :knowledge-point/title "Calculating the Cosine of an Angle"} :step/id #uuid "8bfc4661-356b-5920-8c62-42e9e563ec9c" :step/math-academy-id 21811 :step/next {:db/id 17592186134652}}] :activity/title "The Cauchy-Schwarz Inequality and the Angle Between Two Vectors" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045463 :db/ident :activity.type/lesson} :db/id 17592186133988} {:db/id 17592186134648 :step/content {:db/id 17592186135038 :tutorial/content "The **Cauchy-Schwarz Inequality** (sometimes called the **Cauchy-Bunyakovsky-Schwarz Inequality**) provides a connection between dot products and norms. It states that for any two vectors $\mathbf{u}$ and $\mathbf{v}$ in $\mathbb{R}^n$, we have the inequality

$$
\vert \mathbf{u} \cdot \mathbf{v} \vert \leq \Vert \mathbf{u} \Vert \Vert \mathbf{v} \Vert.
$$

In other words, the absolute value of the dot product is no more than the product of the norms.

For instance, if $[\begin{aligned}3 \\ -4\end{aligned}]$ and $[\begin{aligned}5 \\ 12\end{aligned}]$ then 

$$
\begin{aligned}|u\cdot v| & \le ‖u‖\cdot ‖v‖ \\ |3\cdot 5+(-4)\cdot 12| & \le \sqrt{{3}^{2}+(-4)^{2}}\sqrt{{5}^{2}+{12}^{2}} \\ |-33| & \le 5\cdot 13 \\ 33 & \le 65.\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

**Note:** An easy trick to remember the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality is to think of the formula for the dot product:

$$
\mathbf u \cdot \mathbf v = \Vert \mathbf u \Vert \Vert \mathbf v \Vert \cos \theta
$$

Because $\vert \cos \theta \vert \leq 1,$ we can see that

$$
\vert \mathbf{u} \cdot \mathbf{v} \vert \leq \Vert \mathbf{u} \Vert \Vert \mathbf{v} \Vert.
$$

**Watch out!** The above trick is only a mnemonic trick, *not* an actual proof of the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality. The formula $\mathbf u \cdot \mathbf v = \Vert \mathbf u \Vert \Vert \mathbf v \Vert \cos \theta$ is actually a *consequence* of the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality, so a proof of the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality cannot use the formula." :tutorial/id #uuid "7dd99f48-bbdd-5c22-b5b5-f540eed16b92" :tutorial/math-academy-id 3609 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "37742cc9-b4c6-528d-a58c-980bbc6f6f0f" :step/math-academy-id 20206 :step/next {:db/id 17592186134649}} {:db/id 17592186135038 :tutorial/content "The **Cauchy-Schwarz Inequality** (sometimes called the **Cauchy-Bunyakovsky-Schwarz Inequality**) provides a connection between dot products and norms. ![](images/82/8244d121c65d655f42378c68e1a197528fb2db60a3890b3842e3c93692d88071.png)

To do that, we say that $\cos\theta$ will be equal to the ratio of the two sides of the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality, as follows:

$$
\cos\theta	=	\dfrac{\mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{v}}{\Vert \mathbf{u} \Vert \cdot \Vert \mathbf{v} \Vert}
$$

Notice that this formula is completely analogous to the formula for the angle between two vectors in two-dimensional or three-dimensional space. It only works for non-zero vectors (otherwise, we will be dividing by zero).

Since the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality guarantees that $|\mathbf{u} \cdot \mathbf{v}| \leq \| \mathbf{u} \| \cdot \| \mathbf{v} \|$, we get

$$
-1 \leq \dfrac{\mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{v}}{\Vert \mathbf{u} \Vert \cdot \Vert \mathbf{v} \Vert} \leq 1,
$$

which means that $\theta$ can be found given any two non-zero $\mathbf{u}$ and $\mathbf{v}$." :tutorial/id #uuid "fb193109-edd9-56c5-a643-2472eb776c80" :tutorial/math-academy-id 3610 :tutorial/title "The Angle Between Two Vectors"} :step/id #uuid "26f7bbc7-420d-5194-a4cc-342313c26a2f" :step/math-academy-id 20208 :step/next {:db/id 17592186134651}} {:db/id 17592186135039 :tutorial/content "Now, using the dot product, we can define the angle $\theta$ between two vectors $\mathbf{u}$ and $\mathbf{v}$ in $\mathbb{R}^n$, where $n \ge 2$.

$$
\vert \mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{v} \vert \leq \Vert \mathbf{u} \Vert \Vert \mathbf{v} \Vert
$$

To start, let $t\in\mathbb{R}$ be any number, and consider the vector $t\mathbf{u}+\mathbf{v}.$ Since $\Vert t\mathbf{u} + \mathbf{v} \Vert \geq 0,$ using the definition and properties of the dot product, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}‖tu+v{‖}^{2} & \ge 0 \\ (tu+v)\cdot (tu+v) & \ge 0 \\ {t}^{2}(u\cdot u)+t(u\cdot v)+t(v\cdot u)+(v\cdot v) & \ge 0 \\ {t}^{2}‖u{‖}^{2}+2t(u\cdot v)+‖v{‖}^{2} & \ge 0.\end{aligned}
$$

In the last line above, we have a quadratic with the coefficients $a=\Vert \mathbf{u} \Vert^2,$ $b=2\left( \mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{v} \right),$ and $c=\Vert \mathbf{v} \Vert^2.$

Since the quadratic is greater than or equal to zero, its discriminant must be less than or equal to zero, $\mathcal{D} \leq 0.$ Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}D & \le 0 \\ {b}^{2}-4ac & \le 0 \\ {(2(u\cdot v))}^{2}-4\cdot ‖u{‖}^{2}\cdot ‖v{‖}^{2} & \le 0 \\ 4{(u\cdot v)}^{2}-4‖u{‖}^{2}‖v{‖}^{2} & \le 0 \\ {(u\cdot v)}^{2} & \le ‖u{‖}^{2}‖v{‖}^{2} \\ \sqrt{{(u\cdot v)}^{2}} & \le \sqrt{‖u{‖}^{2}‖v{‖}^{2}} \\ |u\cdot v| & \le ‖u‖‖v‖.\end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "60d5d1df-43c6-5f0a-9f65-0bf4f078cff0" :tutorial/math-academy-id 3614 :tutorial/title "Algebraic Proof of the Schwarz Inequality"} :step/id #uuid "1fa328eb-e089-5fa4-8c20-b79162bc8781" :step/math-academy-id 20213} {:db/id 17592186135041 :tutorial/content "Now, let's prove the general statement of the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality for vectors $\mathbf{u}, \mathbf{v} \in \mathbb{R}^n\mathbin{:}$

$$

$$

To start, let $t\in\mathbb{R}$ be any number, and consider the vector $t\mathbf{u}+\mathbf{v}.$ Since $\Vert t\mathbf{u} + \mathbf{v} \Vert \geq 0,$ using the definition and properties of the dot product, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}‖tu+v{‖}^{2} & \ge 0 \\ (tu+v)\cdot (tu+v) & \ge 0 \\ {t}^{2}(u\cdot u)+t(u\cdot v)+t(v\cdot u)+(v\cdot v) & \ge 0 \\ {t}^{2}‖u{‖}^{2}+2t(u\cdot v)+‖v{‖}^{2} & \ge 0.\end{aligned}
$$

In the last line above, we have a quadratic with the coefficients $a=\Vert \mathbf{u} \Vert^2,$ $b=2\left( \mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{v} \right),$ and $c=\Vert \mathbf{v} \Vert^2.$

Since the quadratic is greater than or equal to zero, its discriminant must be less than or equal to zero, $\mathcal{D} \leq 0.$ Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}D & \le 0 \\ {b}^{2}-4ac & \le 0 \\ {(2(u\cdot v))}^{2}-4\cdot ‖u{‖}^{2}\cdot ‖v{‖}^{2} & \le 0 \\ 4{(u\cdot v)}^{2}-4‖u{‖}^{2}‖v{‖}^{2} & \le 0 \\ {(u\cdot v)}^{2} & \le ‖u{‖}^{2}‖v{‖}^{2} \\ \sqrt{{(u\cdot v)}^{2}} & \le \sqrt{‖u{‖}^{2}‖v{‖}^{2}} \\ |u\cdot v| & \le ‖u‖‖v‖.\end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "60d5d1df-43c6-5f0a-9f65-0bf4f078cff0" :tutorial/math-academy-id 3614 :tutorial/title "Algebraic Proof of the Schwarz Inequality"} {:activity/course {:db/id 17592186046673} :activity/first-step {:db/id 17592186414665} :activity/id #uuid "1cd8eb7e-fe04-5fdd-83e0-383ffc51e2ba" :activity/scope {:db/id 17592186050693 :topic/id #uuid "5f71e968-b382-5c1b-bc8c-518dc0440228" :topic/math-academy-id 2101} :activity/steps [{:db/id 17592186414664 :step/content {:db/id 17592186414663 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "1bec6782-5b25-5f66-a69c-bd940a684008" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{84.32}^{∘}" :db/id 17592186414645} {:answer/id #uuid "42d9c80c-b7ce-5329-bd52-05c6944cc99d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{83.24}^{∘}" :db/id 17592186414648} {:answer/id #uuid "6fccab70-38d0-5196-9e05-328ab9515f03" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{85.50}^{∘}" :db/id 17592186414649} {:answer/id #uuid "82db5a26-f843-545e-b28d-8edda8760ffb" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{87.27}^{∘}" :db/id 17592186414651} {:answer/id #uuid "89bd71bc-8f74-5cc5-8323-858f0ad1097e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{85.35}^{∘}" :db/id 17592186414652}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186414649} :answer-field/id #uuid "c9256cbf-1d22-506c-aaed-b510f33eb670" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186414661}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "99b52f99-8be2-5e57-bfd3-38bdea87dcf3" :question/math-academy-id "q-40563" :question/problem "Rounded to two decimal places, what is the acute angle between the vectors $v=[\begin{aligned}6 \\ \sqrt{5} \\ 1 \\ -1\end{aligned}]$ and $w=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -2 \\ 2\sqrt{5} \\ 3\end{aligned}]?$" :question/worked-solution "Using the formula

$$
\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta =\frac{v\cdot w}{‖v‖\,‖w‖},
$$

we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & =\frac{{v}_{1}{w}_{1}+{v}_{2}{w}_{2}+{v}_{3}{w}_{3}+{v}_{4}{w}_{4}}{\sqrt{{v}_{1}^{2}+{v}_{2}^{2}+{v}_{3}^{2}+{v}_{4}^{2}}\sqrt{{w}_{1}^{2}+{w}_{2}^{2}+{w}_{3}^{2}+{w}_{4}^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{(6)(1)+(\sqrt{5})(-2)+(1)(2\sqrt{5})+(-1)(3)}{\sqrt{{6}^{2}+(\sqrt{5})^{2}+{1}^{2}+(-1)^{2}}\sqrt{{1}^{2}+(-2)^{2}+(2\sqrt{5})^{2}+{3}^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{3}{\sqrt{43}\sqrt{34}} \\  & =\frac{3\sqrt{1462}}{1462}\end{aligned}
$$

 

Therefore, 

$$
\theta =\operatorname{arccos}⁡(\frac{3\sqrt{1462}}{1462})≈{85.50}^{∘}.
$$"} :step/id #uuid "31ec05bc-1755-5418-abd2-881dd5798752" :step/next {:db/id 17592186414666}} {:db/id 17592186414665 :step/content {:db/id 17592186414662 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "2bff7206-3e83-5486-87f5-627306292967" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{\pi }{5}" :db/id 17592186414646} {:answer/id #uuid "385da54c-4492-5bbc-951a-ed5c5080d241" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{\pi }{4}" :db/id 17592186414647} {:answer/id #uuid "c9aa9be2-fd88-5217-83f7-344e4baf419e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{\pi }{3}" :db/id 17592186414656} {:answer/id #uuid "d4a61390-9440-51e4-aed8-0f77831ed9d6" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{\pi }{8}" :db/id 17592186414657} {:answer/id #uuid "faeabdd2-c5d4-509e-96e7-7dc4d046eb5d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{\pi }{6}" :db/id 17592186414658}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186414647} :answer-field/id #uuid "8e595341-6d0b-5218-827a-e206e85ab469" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186414659}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "44f2ea0b-1adf-505c-8fa7-ec801c70c20d" :question/math-academy-id "q-40560" :question/problem "Find the acute angle between the vectors $v=[\begin{aligned}-\sqrt{2} \\ 1 \\ -2 \\ 3\end{aligned}]$ and $w=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ \sqrt{2} \\ -5 \\ 2\end{aligned}].$" :question/worked-solution "Using the formula

$$
\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta =\frac{v\cdot w}{‖v‖\,‖w‖},
$$

we have the following: 

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & =\frac{{v}_{1}{w}_{1}+{v}_{2}{w}_{2}+{v}_{3}{w}_{3}+{v}_{4}{w}_{4}}{\sqrt{{v}_{1}^{2}+{v}_{2}^{2}+{v}_{3}^{2}+{v}_{4}^{2}}\sqrt{{w}_{1}^{2}+{w}_{2}^{2}+{w}_{3}^{2}+{w}_{4}^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{(-\sqrt{2})(1)+(1)(\sqrt{2})+(-2)(-5)+(3)(2)}{\sqrt{(-\sqrt{2})^{2}+{1}^{2}+(-2)^{2}+{3}^{2}}\sqrt{{1}^{2}+(\sqrt{2})^{2}+(-5)^{2}+{2}^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{16}{\sqrt{16}\sqrt{32}} \\  & =\frac{4}{\sqrt{32}} \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, 

$$
\theta =\operatorname{arccos}⁡(\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2})=\frac{\pi }{4}.
$$"} :step/id #uuid "a5f85e51-6089-5f7b-af28-71304b8227fc" :step/next {:db/id 17592186414664}} {:db/id 17592186414666 :step/content {:db/id 17592186134331 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "002742f3-7284-5ac0-8779-30b804e92705" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{3}{\sqrt{131}}" :db/id 17592186414644} {:answer/id #uuid "7d06f1ec-30ff-53f8-9943-6ae3b36ce40d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{9}{\sqrt{266}}" :db/id 17592186414650} {:answer/id #uuid "bcaffc6f-0a85-5982-a4c7-707c5cbc1a65" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{15}{\sqrt{131}}" :db/id 17592186414653} {:answer/id #uuid "bd84ff6d-55f1-5a15-aef5-c63480bc1877" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{13}{\sqrt{266}}" :db/id 17592186414654} {:answer/id #uuid "bf2d35a4-2976-51e9-ab5e-f0e748e55003" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{18}{\sqrt{266}}" :db/id 17592186414655}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186414650} :answer-field/id #uuid "c90a5531-3cd5-5504-b1c0-5278d3ea6ed7" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186414660}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "3dd6a25a-12e9-5ca9-91cb-a545462d6da3" :question/math-academy-id "q-40902" :question/problem "Let $A(-2,1,0,-3)$ and $B(1,-1,1,-4).$ Find the cosine of the angle $∠AOB$, where $O(0,0,0,0)$ is the origin." :question/worked-solution "First, let

$$
\begin{aligned}a=\overset{\to }{OA}=[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 1 \\ 0 \\ -3\end{aligned}],\,b=\overset{\to }{OB}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1 \\ 1 \\ -4\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Also, let $\theta =m∠AOB$ be the angle between the vectors $a$ and $b.$ Then, we can find $\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta $ using the following formula:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & =\frac{a\cdot b}{‖a‖\,‖b‖} \\  & =\frac{{a}_{1}{b}_{1}+{a}_{2}{b}_{2}+{a}_{3}{b}_{3}+{a}_{4}{b}_{4}}{\sqrt{{a}_{1}^{2}+{a}_{2}^{2}+{a}_{3}^{2}+{a}_{4}^{2}}\,\sqrt{{b}_{1}^{2}+{b}_{2}^{2}+{b}_{3}^{2}+{b}_{4}^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{(-2)\cdot 1+1\cdot (-1)+0\cdot 1+(-3)\cdot (-4)}{\sqrt{(-2)^{2}+{1}^{2}+{0}^{2}+(-3)^{2}}\,\sqrt{{1}^{2}+(-1)^{2}+{1}^{2}+(-4)^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{9}{\sqrt{14}\cdot \sqrt{19}} \\  & =\frac{9}{\sqrt{266}}\end{aligned}

$$
(6y(x - 2))/(9yz) = (2 \cdot 3 \cdot y \cdot (x - 2))/(3 \cdot 3 \cdot y \cdot z)
$$

Then, we cancel out all the pairs of common factors in the numerator and denominator. In this case, there is one pair of $3$'s and one pair of $y$'s.

$$
\begin{aligned}
(2 \cdot 3 \cdot y \cdot (x - 2))/(3 \cdot 3 \cdot y \cdot z) &=  \\
(2 \cdot 3 \cdot y \cdot (x - 2))/(3 \cdot 3 \cdot y \cdot z) &=  \\
(2 \cdot (x - 2))/(3z) &=  \\
&= (2(x - 2))/(3z)
\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, the expression simplifies to

$$
\dfrac{2(x - 2)}{3z}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186055413 :question/id #uuid "53cd820c-14bd-540b-b6a2-c7ae2dae8ef0" :question/math-academy-id "q-57730"} {:db/id 17592186055414 :question/id #uuid "12123fa2-8aaa-5056-8a04-21f6d757b498" :question/math-academy-id "q-57733"} {:db/id 17592186054691 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186054591 :question/id #uuid "d076b225-6e63-592e-b03e-2986c1f7685c" :question/math-academy-id "e-839"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "19e1ac67-8538-5f72-bb0d-b7e4adda36a7" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186050998}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186055271 :question/id #uuid "e27b0afe-a600-5fe7-a61f-9c2da9263c61" :question/math-academy-id "q-41562"} {:db/id 17592186055464 :question/id #uuid "4ecf67fa-d3f8-5cc1-8118-9551714ce1b1" :question/math-academy-id "q-687"}] :knowledge-point/title "Simplifying Rational Expressions with Common Binomial Factors"} {:db/id 17592186054591 :question/id #uuid "d076b225-6e63-592e-b03e-2986c1f7685c" :question/math-academy-id "e-839" :knowledge-point/_canonical-example [{:db/id 17592186054691 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "19e1ac67-8538-5f72-bb0d-b7e4adda36a7" :knowledge-point/title "Simplifying Rational Expressions with Common Binomial Factors"}] :question/problem "Simplify $\dfrac{6a(c+1)}{3b(c+1)}$." :question/worked-solution "First, we decompose all of the terms into their prime factors. $$

$$
\begin{aligned}
(2 \cdot 2 \cdot 5)/(2 \cdot 2 \cdot 2 \cdot (z - 1)) &=  \\
(2 \cdot 2 \cdot 5)/(2 \cdot 2 \cdot 2 \cdot (z - 1)) &=  \\

&= (5)/(2(z - 1))
\end{aligned}
$$

:activity/steps [{:db/id 17592186055660 :step/content {:db/id 17592186055937 :tutorial/content "If a rational expression is expressed in factored form, we can sometimes make the expression even simpler by pulling out factors that are common in both the numerator and denominator.

For example, suppose that we want to simplify the rational expression

$$
\dfrac{4(2x-3)}{2}
$$

If we decompose $4$ into $2\cdot 2$, we can pull out a factor of $2$ from both the numerator and denominator:

$$
\begin{aligned}
(4(2x - 3))/(2) &=  \\
(2 \cdot 2 \cdot (2x - 3))/(2) &=  \\
&= \frac{2}{2} \cdot (2 \cdot (2x - 3))/(1)
\end{aligned}
$$

The fraction

$$
\dfrac{2}{2}
$$

is the same as $1$, and anything times $1$ is just itself, so

$$
\begin{aligned}
\frac{2}{2} \cdot (2 \cdot (2x - 3))/(1) &=  \\
1 \cdot (2 \cdot (2x - 3))/(1) &=  \\
&= (2 \cdot (2x - 3))/(1) \\
&= 2(2x - 3)
\end{aligned}
$$

**Note:** There is a shortcut! We can just "cancel" a $2$ from the numerator and denominator.

$$
\begin{aligned}
(4(2x - 3))/(2) &=  \\
(2 \cdot 2 \cdot (2x - 3))/(2) &=  \\
(2 \cdot 2 \cdot (2x - 3))/(2) &=  \\
(2 \cdot (2x - 3))/(1) &=  \\
&= 2(2x - 3)
\end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "5a1da69d-c5e3-5832-9f42-e75315b6c1a4" :tutorial/math-academy-id 1369 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "f4f7f7d8-d9a6-5429-90e3-be9b91605346" :step/math-academy-id 17592186045486 :db/ident :question.difficulty/hard} :question/problem "Suppose that a function $f(x,y,z)$ and all of its higher-order partial derivatives are continuous on an open set $U,$ and that

$$
\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}}=(x{y}^{2}+2y){e}^{xy}+2{z}^{3},\,\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂z}=6x{z}^{2}.
$$

 

Evaluate the following expression at the point $(1,0,1):$

$$
\frac{{∂}^{3}f}{∂x∂y∂x}+\frac{{∂}^{3}f}{∂z∂x∂z}
$$" :question/worked-solution "As the higher-order partial derivatives are continuous on an open set $U,$ the mixed partial derivatives must be equal. 

Hence, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{3}f}{∂x∂y∂x} & =\frac{{∂}^{3}f}{∂y∂{x}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}}) \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂y}((x{y}^{2}+2y){e}^{xy}+2{z}^{3}) \\  & =(x{y}^{2}+2y)\cdot x{e}^{xy}+(2xy+2)\cdot {e}^{xy}+0 \\  & =({x}^{2}{y}^{2}+4xy+2){e}^{xy}.\end{aligned}
$$

In addition, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{3}f}{∂z∂x∂z} & =\frac{∂}{∂z}(\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂z}) \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂z}(6x{z}^{2}) \\  & =12xz.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we evaluate both partial derivatives at the point $(1,0,1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{3}f}{∂x∂y∂x}{|}_{(1,0,1)} & =(0+0+2){e}^{0}=2 \\ \frac{{∂}^{3}f}{∂z∂x∂z}{|}_{(1,0,1)} & =12(1)(1)=12\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{3}f}{∂x∂y∂x}{|}_{(1,0,1)}+\frac{{∂}^{3}f}{∂z∂x∂z}{|}_{(1,0,1)} & =2+12=14.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186268928 :question/id #uuid "f5acd057-670a-5a23-995b-650a92790dc3" :question/math-academy-id "q-133371"} {:db/id 17592186268929 :question/id #uuid ${f}_{yxy}(1,0)-{f}_{yy}(1,0)-{f}_{xyy}(1,0)$ given that ${f}_{yy}(x,y)={x}^{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡xy?$" :question/worked-solution "As the function and its first, second, and third-order partial derivatives are continuous on an open set $U,$ we must have ${f}_{yxy}(x,y)={f}_{xyy}(x,y).$ 

Therefore, we can swap the order of the subscripts in the first term. This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{yxy}(1,0)-{f}_{yy}(1,0)-{f}_{xyy}(1,0) & ={f}_{xyy}(1,0)-{f}_{yy}(1,0)-{f}_{xyy}(1,0) \\  & =\cancel{{f}_{xyy}(1,0)}-{f}_{yy}(1,0)-\cancel{{f}_{xyy}(1,0)} \\  & =-{f}_{yy}(1,0) \\  & =-(1)^{3}\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡(1\cdot 0) \\  & =-1\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡0 \\  & =-1.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186409651 :question/id #uuid "923e8280-3481-5e90-8081-225a78ef2cea" :question/math-academy-id "q-133393" :knowledge-point/_questions [{:db/id 17592186124449 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "a7619454-7a2b-5c0b-927c-24dca2e564c3" :knowledge-point/title "Evaluating Expressions of Partial Derivatives at a Point"}] :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "4421a8c6-aea6-5d62-9cd0-8a06f8915dcd" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "2" :db/id 17592186409638} {:answer/id #uuid "45730328-f0dc-5c33-a6c2-53d71d04445d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "1" :db/id 17592186409639} {:answer/id #uuid "4d58c242-f6fd-5d67-8e96-0273fcae35a5" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "0" :db/id 17592186409641} {:answer/id #uuid "59fd5070-c975-5965-b9d4-d62ba5834853" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "3" :db/id 17592186409642} {:answer/id #uuid "d26ca855-4a28-50fd-bba1-040fec87c89e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "5" :db/id 17592186409647}] :answer-field/correct {:answer/id #uuid "59fd5070-c975-5965-b9d4-d62ba5834853" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "3" :db/id 17592186409642} :answer-field/id #uuid "504a276b-9fed-5959-a86c-c2b987992901" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493 :db/ident :answer-field.type/radio} :db/id 17592186409648}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487 :db/ident :question.difficulty/moderate} :question/problem "Evaluate ${f}_{zxz}(2,\frac{1}{2},1)$ given that a function $f(x,y,z)$ and all of its higher-order partial derivatives are continuous on an open set $U,$ and that

$$
{f}_{zz}(x,y,z)=2z\operatorname{ln}⁡(x-2y)+x{e}^{z-2y}
$$" :question/worked-solution "As the higher-order partial derivatives are continuous on an open set $U,$ the mixed partial derivatives must be equal. 

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{zzx}(x,y,z) & ={f}_{zxz}(x,y,z) \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({f}_{zz}(x,y,z)) \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(2z\operatorname{ln}⁡(x-2y)+x{e}^{z-2y}) \\  & =2z\cdot \frac{1}{x-2y}+{e}^{z-2y} \\  & =\frac{2z}{x-2y}+{e}^{z-2y}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we evaluate the partial derivative at the point  $(2,\frac{1}{2},1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{zxz}(2,\frac{1}{2},1) & =\frac{2\cdot 1}{2-2\cdot \frac{1}{2}}+{e}^{1-2\cdot 1/2} \\  & =\frac{2}{2-1}+{e}^{1-1} \\  & =2+1 \\  & =3\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186437088 :question/id #uuid "17f2fd35-823f-52a1-8bc6-17fa0dd0fd8c" :question/math-academy-id "q-133394"} {:db/id 17592186124450 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186408166} :db/id 17592186460804}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/problem "Suppose that the function $f(x,y)$ and all of its first and second-order partial derivatives are continuous on an open set $U.$ Which of the following pairs could represent the first-order partial derivatives of $f(x,y)?$
- **I.** ${f}_{x}(x,y)=x+4y$ and ${f}_{y}(x,y)=3x-y$
- **II.** ${f}_{x}(x,y)=2x$ and ${f}_{y}(x,y)=0$
- **III.** ${f}_{x}(x,y)=2x+\operatorname{cos}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡y$ and ${f}_{y}(x,y)={e}^{y}-\operatorname{sin}⁡x\operatorname{sin}⁡y$

Select all that apply." :question/worked-solution "Since the function and its first and second-order partial derivatives are continuous on an open set $U,$ the mixed partial derivatives must be equal, that is, ${f}_{xy}(x,y)={f}_{yx}(x,y).$ Let's check if this condition is true for each of our pairs of first-order partial derivatives.

- For the first pair, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{xy}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(x+4y)=4 \\ {f}_{yx}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(3x-y)=3.\end{aligned}
$$

As ${f}_{xy}(x,y)\ne {f}_{yx}(x,y)$, the first pair cannot represent the first-order partial derivatives of $f(x,y).$

- For the second pair, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{xy}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(2x)=0 \\ {f}_{yx}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(0)=0.\end{aligned}
$$

As ${f}_{xy}(x,y)={f}_{yx}(x,y)$, the second pair could represent the first-order partial derivatives of $f(x,y).$

- For the third pair, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{xy}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(2x+\operatorname{cos}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡y) \\  & =0+\operatorname{cos}⁡x\cdot (-\operatorname{sin}⁡y) \\  & =-\operatorname{cos}⁡x\operatorname{sin}⁡y, \\ {f}_{yx}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({e}^{y}-\operatorname{sin}⁡x\operatorname{sin}⁡y) \\  & =0-\operatorname{sin}⁡y\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡x \\  & =-\operatorname{cos}⁡x\operatorname{sin}⁡y.\end{aligned}
$$

As ${f}_{xy}(x,y)={f}_{yx}(x,y)$,  the third pair could represent the first-order partial derivatives of $f(x,y).$

Therefore, the correct answer is 'II and III only'."} {:db/id 17592186125186 :question/id #uuid "3caf1655-4ce4-5a5f-995b-a06e33069b3a" :question/math-academy-id "q-65127"} {:db/id 17592186268926 \begin{aligned}{f}_{xy}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({e}^{-2x}-y)=-1 \\ {f}_{yx}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({e}^{-y}-2x)=-2.\end{aligned}

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{xy}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({e}^{x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x)=0 \\ {f}_{yx}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(5)=0.\end{aligned}
$$

As ${f}_{xy}(x,y)={f}_{yx}(x,y)$, the second pair could represent the first-order partial derivatives of $f(x,y).$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{xy}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(2{y}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡xy+{y}^{2})=4y\operatorname{cos}⁡xy-2x{y}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡xy+2y \\ {f}_{yx}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(2\operatorname{sin}⁡xy+2xy\operatorname{cos}⁡xy+2xy) \\  & =2y\operatorname{cos}⁡xy+2y\operatorname{cos}⁡xy-2x{y}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡xy+2y \\  & =4y\operatorname{cos}⁡xy-2x{y}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡xy+2y.\end{aligned}
$$

As ${f}_{xy}(x,y)={f}_{yx}(x,y)$,  the third pair could represent the first-order partial derivatives of $f(x,y).$

derivatives are

$$
\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x} (x,y) = y^2 -3x^2y \quad \mathrm{and} \quad \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial y}(x,y) = 2xy -x^3,
$$

and the second-order **mixed partial derivatives** are 

$$
\dfrac{\partial^2 f}{\partial y\, \partial x}(x,y) = 2y -3x^2 \quad \mathrm{and} \quad  \dfrac{\partial^2 f}{\partial x\, \partial y}(x,y) = 2y-3x^2.
$$

Notice that these two mixed partial derivatives are equal, i.e., 

$$
\dfrac{\partial^2 f}{\partial y\, \partial x}=\dfrac{\partial^2 f}{\partial x\, \partial y}.
$$

In general, if a function $f(x,y)$ has continuous first-order partial derivatives on an open set $U,$ and the second-order mixed partial derivatives exist and are continuous on $U,$ then the mixed partial derivatives are equal everywhere on $U.$" :tutorial/id #uuid "96f3873b-8f1b-5481-827e-503e557bbe9c" :tutorial/math-academy-id 2408 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid function whose first-order and second-order mixed partial derivatives are continuous on an open set $U,$ then the second-order mixed partial derivatives are equal everywhere on $U.$

$$
\dfrac{\partial^2 f}{\partial x\, \partial y} =\dfrac{\partial^2 f}{\partial y\, \partial x}
$$

This result also extends to higher-order partial derivatives. For example, if the third-order partial derivatives of $f(x,y)$ are also continuous everywhere on $U,$ then the third-order mixed partial derivatives are independent of the order in which the differentiation is performed. 

For example,

$$
\dfrac{\partial^3 f}{\color{blue}\partial x\, \partial x\, \partial y} =\dfrac{\partial^3 f}{\color{red}\partial y\, \partial x \, \partial x}.
$$

In this case, we can think of $\color{blue}\partial x\, \partial x\, \partial y$ and $\color{red}\partial y\, \partial x \, \partial x$ as distinct permutations of the symbols $\partial x,\partial x,$ and $\partial y.$ Any permutation of these symbols gives the same result. For example,

$$
\dfrac{\partial^3 f}{\color{blue}\partial x\, \partial x\, \partial y} = \dfrac{\partial^3 f}{\color{purple}\partial x\, \partial y\, \partial x}.
$$

**Watch out!** This does **not** mean that *all* third partial derivatives are equal! For example, it is generally true that

$$
\dfrac{\partial^3 f}{\color{blue}\partial x\, \partial x\, \partial y} \neq \dfrac{\partial^3 f}{\partial x\, \partial y\, \partial y}.
$$
